caveat.notSame: Note: “not significant” does not mean “the same” – a small sample can hide a difference.
caveat.cause: The result describes an association, not a cause.
caveat.expected: The test assumes expected counts of at least 5 in most cells.

ttest.indSig: **{{variable}}** **differs significantly** between the groups – it is higher for {{higher}} ({{stats}}).
ttest.diffSig: The difference of {{diff}} in favour of {{higher}} is {{size}} (d = {{d}}).
ttest.leveneOk: Levene's test ({{p}}) does not suggest unequal variances, so the first table row applies.
ttest.leveneWelch: Levene's test ({{p}}) shows unequal variances, so the second table row (Welch's test) applies.
ttest.pairedNs: There is **no significant difference** between **{{a}}** and **{{b}}** ({{stats}}).
ttest.pairedDiff: The mean change of {{diff}} is a {{size}} effect (dz = {{d}}).
ttest.oneSig: The mean of **{{variable}}** ({{mean}}) is significantly **{{dir}}** than {{value}} ({{stats}}).
ttest.oneNs: The mean of **{{variable}}** ({{mean}}) does **not differ significantly** from {{value}} ({{stats}}).
ttest.oneDetail: M = {{mean}}, SD = {{sd}}, n = {{n}}; the difference is {{size}} (d = {{d}}).

anova.sig: The means of **{{variable}}** **differ significantly** between the groups ({{stats}}).
anova.ns: The means of **{{variable}}** do **not differ significantly** between the groups ({{stats}}).
anova.range: The highest mean is in {{hi}} ({{mhi}}), the lowest in {{lo}} ({{mlo}}).
anova.eta: The groups explain {{pct}} % of the variance (η² = {{eta}}), a {{size}} effect.
anova.posthoc: A post hoc test (e.g. Tukey) in the ANOVA dialog shows which groups differ.
anova.levene: Levene's test ({{p}}) shows unequal variances – treat the result with care, or use the Kruskal-Wallis test.

corr.noneSig_other: None of the {{count}} correlations is significant.
corr.posMeaning: A positive relationship means higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other.

crosstab.sig: There **is a significant association** between the variables in **{{title}}** ({{stats}}).
crosstab.ns: There is **no significant association** between the variables in **{{title}}** ({{stats}}).

reg.r2: Together the predictors explain {{pct}} % of the variance of {{dependent}}.
reg.pred: {{name}}: each extra unit {{dir}} the prediction by {{b}} ({{stats}}).

freq.top: The most frequent value of **{{variable}}** is **{{top}}** ({{pct}} % of valid answers).

mw.sig: **{{variable}}** **differs significantly** between the groups – {{higher}} has higher ranks ({{stats}}).
mw.ns: **{{variable}}** does **not differ significantly** between the groups ({{stats}}).

kw.ns: **{{variable}}** does **not differ significantly** between the groups ({{stats}}).

wx.sig: There **is a significant difference** between the measurements **{{label}}** ({{stats}}).
wx.ns: There is **no significant difference** between the measurements **{{label}}** ({{stats}}).

chi1.sig: The categories of **{{variable}}** are **not equally represented** ({{stats}}).
chi1.ns: The distribution of **{{variable}}** does **not differ significantly** from an even one ({{stats}}).
chi1.detail: {{over}} is most above expectation, {{under}} most below.

rel.line: Cronbach's alpha is **{{alpha}}** for {{items}} items – internal consistency is **{{quality}}**.
rel.detail: Values from .70 are usually considered acceptable, from .80 good.
rel.tooHigh: An alpha above .95 may mean the items are redundant.

assistant.title: Analysis guide
assistant.subtitle: Say what you want to find out and PSPP Studio recommends a suitable test.
assistant.step1: What do you want to find out?
assistant.fillSlots: Choose variables on the left and the recommendation appears here.

why.describeCat: Categorical variables are best described by frequency tables and a bar chart.
why.describeScale: For scale variables you want the mean, spread and shape – Explore shows statistics, a histogram and a boxplot.
why.describeMixed: Categorical variables get frequencies, scale variables the mean, standard deviation and a histogram.
why.ttest: Two groups ({{group}}) and a scale variable → the independent-samples t-test compares the means.
why.mwOrdinal: An ordinal variable and two groups ({{group}}) → the Mann-Whitney test compares ranks instead of means.
why.anova: {{k}} groups ({{group}}) and a scale variable → one-way ANOVA; a post hoc test (Tukey) shows which groups differ.
why.kwOrdinal: {{k}} groups ({{group}}) and an ordinal variable → the Kruskal-Wallis test.
why.crosstabs: Both variables are categorical → a crosstabulation with the chi-square test.
why.paired: Two measurements of the same people → the paired t-test compares the mean change.
why.wilcoxonOrdinal: Two ordinal measurements of the same people → the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
why.friedman: {{k}} measurements of the same people → the Friedman test.
why.relateNominal: Categorical variables → a crosstabulation and chi-square with the strength of association (Cramér's V).
why.pearson: Scale variables → Pearson correlation; a scatterplot shows the shape of the relationship.
why.spearman: At least one variable is ordinal → Spearman correlation.
why.logistic: {{name}} has two values → binary logistic regression.
why.multinomial: A nominal outcome with several categories is shown as a crosstabulation for now.
why.glm: A scale outcome and categorical predictors → the general linear model (ANOVA with several factors).
why.regression: A scale outcome ({{name}}) → linear regression shows how the predictors affect it.
why.distribution: A histogram, Q-Q plot and normality tests in Explore show whether the distribution is roughly normal.
why.reliability: {{k}} items of one scale → Cronbach's alpha with item-total statistics.
why.oneSample: The mean of one variable against {{value}} → the one-sample t-test.

assume.independent: Each person is in one group only (independent samples).
assume.normal: The variable is roughly normal in each group (with n ≥ 30 small deviations do not matter).
assume.levene: Similar variances in the groups – Levene's test is in the output.
assume.expected5: Expected counts of at least 5 in most cells.
assume.samePeople: The measurements belong to the same people (paired data).
assume.normalDiff: The differences between measurements are roughly normal.
assume.monotonic: The relationship is monotonic (one rises or falls with the other).
assume.linear: The relationship is roughly linear – check the scatterplot.
assume.multicol: The predictors are not too strongly correlated.
assume.events: Enough cases in both categories (at least 10 per predictor).
assume.largeN: With large samples normality tests come out “significant” even for small deviations – look mainly at the plots.
assume.sameDirection: All items point in the same direction (recode reversed items first).

alt.nonNormal: If the data are not normal or a group is small (n < 30).
alt.nonNormalDiff: If the differences are not normal or the data are ordinal.
alt.repeatedGlm: Repeated measures with normal data can also be analysed in syntax (GLM with WSFACTOR).
alt.outliers: If there are outliers or the relationship is not linear.
alt.ks: If you want a formal test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov).
alt.factor: To check whether the items form a single factor.
alt.descriptivesTable: If one compact table is enough.

warn.manyGroups: The variable has many groups – is it really categorical?
warn.noMultinomial: PSPP has no multinomial regression yet.
warn.dummy: Nominal predictors with more than two categories need dummy (0/1) variables.
warn.fewItems: Reliability is usually computed from at least three items.
warn.tinyGroups: Very small groups (under 5 % of cases) are left out; the t-test compares the two main groups.
